Episode 4 failed because it **crushed the can**: SafeGrip was off, so nothing capped the grip force — the thumb spiked to 36.0 N, 2.5× the warehouse limit of 14.4 N for a can, and the can fractured at 2.56 s.

The chain of failure:
- **No force cap** — SafeGrip off meant the controller kept squeezing past the safe limit.
- **Bad grip shape** — the palm (thenar) had zero contact, so the entire load rode on 3 fingertips and the thumb took the full spike.
- **Warning ignored** — slip-band vibration appeared on the thumb at 2.61 s, but by then the can was already breaking.

The proof it was preventable: its SafeGrip twin, episode_0000 (same grasp, force limiting on), **succeeded**. Readiness score was 53/100.

Want me to chart the two force curves side by side, or run the certified report on the twin?

With SafeGrip on (episode_0000, the same grasp), it's a **clean success — 100/100 readiness**. Force limiting capped the grip at ~1.2 N per fingertip instead of the 36.0 N spike, and the can came through intact.

| Metric | Episode 4 (SafeGrip off) | Episode 0 (SafeGrip on) |
|---|---|---|
| Outcome | fracture @ 2.56 s | success (12.2 s) |
| Peak force | 36.0 N (thumb) | 1.24 N (index) |
| vs 14.4 N limit | 2.5× over | 8% of limit |
| Slip vibration | 0.21 s (too late) | none |
| Readiness | 53/100 | 100/100 |



Notes:
- Same grasp, same can — the only difference is the force cap. That's the cleanest A/B in the dataset.
- Interesting detail: with SafeGrip on, the thumb and palm never even engaged — index + middle held it gently. The off-twin's failure came from an aggressive 3-fingertip squeeze.
- Friction margin 0.965, 0 ms touch latency, 22.5 cm lift — no other issues at all.

Next steps:
1. This pair is your best exhibit for a "SafeGrip always on" policy — I can pull fleet-wide numbers to back it up.
2. Want the certified readiness report for episode_0000 (0.1 FET)? A 100/100 is a good one to certify.

Notes:
- **Warehouse is the most forgiving handler (53)** — its 14.4 N can limit is the loosest; surgical's 9 N is strictest, so it flags the same force as a 50% safety-factor violation.
- **Quadruped (88) is the interesting outlier:** it doesn't grasp, so a crushed can doesn't matter — it just reads the slip-band vibration as a good foot-slip signal.
- **Sensor QA at 100** means the failure is purely control, not sensing — the glove saw everything in time.

Next steps:
1. This is episode 4's pattern again (crushed can, SafeGrip off) — want me to check whether episode 12 has a SafeGrip-on twin that succeeds?
2. If you're choosing an application for this gripper, the data says: fine for quadruped foot contact, needs SafeGrip for anything that holds objects.
ask the quadruped agent about slip

The quadruped agent's verdict: **episode 12 is actually a demonstration of the slip detector working well** — the 88/100 reflects that the only fault (the can fracturing) is a grip-force problem the quadruped profile doesn't judge, while the slip-band signature itself is clean and usable. One correction to my earlier readout: slip onset was at **2.81 s** (0.206 s duration), not 2.61 s.

**How slip detection works** (mechanism, general knowledge): a pod shows slip when sustained vibration energy in the slip band occurs *while* bearing normal force — distinct from the one-off broadband thump of touchdown. The 350 Hz sampling (175 Hz Nyquist) captures the band directly, with IMUs corroborating. The four pods map to four feet, so slip-band vibration on one pod = that paw sliding during stance — exactly the early warning a gait controller needs.

**Pod-by-pod (feet) for episode 12:**

| Pod (foot) | Peak force | Contact | Slip vibration | Rail frames | Noise vs spec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Front-right (thumb) | 34.84 N | 7.05 s | **0.206 s from 2.81 s** | 0 | 1.01 |
| Front-left | 13.34 N | 6.57 s | 0 | 0 | 1.01 |
| Rear-left | 11.62 N | 6.11 s | 0 | 0 | 1.01 |
| Rear-right | 0 N | never | — | 0 | 1.01 |



**Why the signal is high quality:** it fired only on the pod that slipped, lasted ~0.2 s (well past impact-transient length), sat at spec noise with zero saturation, 0.0 ms touch latency. Notably it began ~80 ms *after* the fracture at 2.73 s — consistent with the can wall crumpling and sliding against the pad, with the high friction margin (0.992) suggesting localized slip rather than gross sliding.



**Why 88 and not 20:** manipulation applications all scored 20 because of the fracture; quadruped scores foot-contact phenomena (slip, impact, contact timing, saturation), which were all clean. The 34.8 N peak only matters to force-limited profiles — force levels don't carry over to feet.

The agent also confirmed the fracture was predictable: across all 32 can recordings, SafeGrip-off succeeds only 25% vs 68.8% with it on — and this episode's SafeGrip twin, **episode_0008**, succeeded.



Next steps it offered: (1) chart the raw slip-band trace around 2.6–3.0 s to show onset shape, (2) pull crush episodes where slip fired *without* fracture as genuine paw-slide analogues, or (3) benchmark slip-detection latency across all 192 recordings.

Notes:
- **Episode_0005 is the one to watch:** 520 saturated frames on a can grasp that also fractured — likely the crush spike drove the magnetometer past range. If you're building a training set, that episode's force values are clipped and should be flagged or excluded.
- **The 57.1 ms worst-case latency** is worth a look if your control loop needs sub-50 ms touch reaction — median is 0.0 ms, so it's rare, but I can find which episode it was.
- **Calibration caveat:** all force numbers are on the assumed 1.5 mT/N scale until a load-cell calibration pass is done — treat absolute N as provisional, ratios (like SafeGrip on/off) as solid.

Next steps:

2. Find the 57.1 ms latency episode and check whether it correlates with a specific scenario.
3. If you're curating data for training, I can flag railed/latency outliers as an exclusion list.
what data should we collect next

Collect **failure-mode diversity and property variation** — not more nominal successes. Touch already lifts grasp macro-F1 from 0.61 (IMU-only) to 0.69, but fault detection sits at just 0.56, and that's exactly where the data is starved: only 9 slip events, 1 impact, and a drop scenario that never succeeds. (Simulated data; 0 hardware recordings so far.)



**The gaps, with evidence:**

| Gap | Evidence | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Slip | 9/192 outcomes, 8 from the bottle in light_grip only | Most actionable failure (reactive tightening), barely covered |
| Impact | 1 recording in the entire set | Fault classifier can't learn collision transients |
| Drop scenario | 48 recordings, **0% success**, 37 early_release | One constant failure mode = almost no discriminative signal |
| Object↔property confound | One (mass, μ) pair per object (e.g. bottle = 520 g, μ 0.45) | Model memorizes "bottle = heavy" instead of "heavy = grip harder" |
| SafeGrip on soft objects | Sponge: 0.50 success with SafeGrip vs 0.69 without (8 incomplete) | Force limiting seems to block conformal grips — needs diagnosis recordings |
| Saturation | episode_0005 (can crush) has 520 railed frames | Corrupts force labels in exactly the high-force episodes that teach crush limits |

**Priority recording plan (from the data curator agent):**
1. **Slip set (~40–60):** low-μ objects, wet/oiled surfaces, slip induced mid-lift — targets the fault-F1 bottleneck directly.
2. **Drop-recovery set (~30–40):** catches and re-grasps at varied heights, so drop becomes two-class.
3. **Property sweep (~60):** vary mass (bottle at 100/250/520 g fill), friction, deformability within each object — highest leverage for generalization.
4. **Impact transients (~20):** bumps, collisions, set-down events.
5. **SafeGrip-on-soft diagnosis (~15):** adaptive force limits to fix the sponge incompletes.
6. **First hardware batch (~20–30) + load-cell calibration** to replace the assumed 1.5 mT/N and quantify sim-to-real shift.

Next steps:
1. I can turn this into a concrete episode-count grid (object × scenario × SafeGrip) ready to hand to whoever runs the sessions.
2. Or drill into the 9 existing slip episodes to define the tactile labeling signature before you collect more.
3. If hardware is imminent, I'd start with the calibration batch — every absolute force number is provisional until then.
